prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: moving spoken dialogue systems beyond turn-based, half-duplex interaction toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex behavior with overlaps, backchannels, and latency-aware turn-taking. The central idea is to adapt a pretrained autoregressive LLM into a “synchronous” dialogue model by injecting periodic timing markers, training on interleaved dual-speaker speech-unit sequences, and using short-horizon prediction of the interlocutor’s current chunk to compensate for real-time latency. The paper also proposes a pragmatic three-stage training recipe that relies heavily on synthetic spoken dialogue derived from text corpora, followed by limited real dual-channel dialogue fine-tuning. Empirically, the work reports substantial gains over dGSLM in semantic meaningfulness while maintaining comparable or slightly improved naturalness, and demonstrates simulated interaction under chunk-level latency.

Overall, I found the paper ambitious, timely, and conceptually interesting. The problem formulation is compelling: most “voice LLM” systems are indeed still fundamentally turn-based, and the paper correctly identifies synchrony and latency as first-class modeling issues rather than mere engineering details. The proposed representation—deduplicated HuBERT tokens plus periodic synchronization tokens—is elegant in its simplicity, and the latency-tolerant inference scheme is intuitive and plausibly useful. The empirical results, especially the large human-rated meaningfulness gains over dGSLM, suggest that leveraging text-pretrained LLMs is a promising direction for spoken dialogue generation. At the same time, several aspects of the methodology and evaluation leave important questions unanswered, and some of the strongest claims are only partially supported by the current evidence.

The main strength of the paper is the framing and architectural reduction. Rather than designing a bespoke duplex architecture, the authors show how to cast full-duplex dialogue as standard autoregressive next-token prediction over a carefully constructed interleaved sequence. This is appealing because it inherits the scaling and semantic strengths of text LLMs. The periodic speaker/synchronization tokens are a neat mechanism for giving the model a coarse notion of wall-clock progression. The deduplication strategy is also sensible: repeated speech-unit tokens are known to dilute semantic density, and the paper gives a reasonable argument for preserving timing coarsely via chunk markers while modeling content on deduplicated units. This combination is one of the more novel technical contributions in the paper.

A second major strength is the training recipe. The three-stage progression from text/speech alignment, to synthetic full-duplex-with-silence formatting, to real spoken dialogue fine-tuning is well motivated by data scarcity. The scale mismatch between text dialogue and real dual-channel spoken dialogue is real, and the paper offers a practical way to exploit abundant text resources. The reported out-of-distribution behavior on CANDOR is also encouraging, especially relative to dGSLM. If robust, this would be a meaningful result: it suggests that text-pretrained semantics plus modest spoken fine-tuning may generalize better than speech-only dialogue models.

The human evaluation is another positive aspect. The paper does not rely solely on automatic metrics, and the distinction between meaningfulness and naturalness is appropriate for this task. The MOS results show a striking gap in meaningfulness between SyncLLM and dGSLM, while naturalness remains roughly comparable. This aligns with the paper’s thesis that text-pretrained LLMs bring stronger semantic competence without sacrificing turn-taking quality too much. The inclusion of both in-domain and OOD subsets is also useful.

That said, the paper has several weaknesses that limit my confidence in the conclusions. The most important issue is that the evaluation of “full-duplex” capability remains indirect. Much of the evidence comes from continuation generation rather than actual interactive deployment with humans. Even the interaction setting is simulated as LLM-LLM interaction with one-chunk latency, not human-agent interaction over a real streaming stack. This is understandable as a first step, but it weakens the central claim that the system functions as a full-duplex dialogue agent in realistic settings. The paper repeatedly emphasizes Internet-scale latency tolerance and real-time synchrony, yet there is no end-to-end latency breakdown, no measurement of actual streaming inference timing, and no user study involving live interaction. As a result, the work demonstrates a promising modeling framework for full-duplex dialogue generation, but not yet a convincing full-duplex deployed agent.

Relatedly, the latency-tolerant inference mechanism is clever but under-evaluated. The model predicts an estimated user chunk for the current time step and then conditions on it to generate its own next chunk, later replacing the estimate with the real user chunk. This is a strong design choice with potentially significant failure modes: compounding errors, instability under misprediction, and sensitivity to chunk size or user unpredictability. However, the paper does not isolate this mechanism in ablations. For example, how much does performance degrade if one simply waits for the real chunk? How much gain comes from anticipation versus from the synchronous tokenization alone? How often is the estimated user chunk wrong in semantically important ways, and how robust is the model to such errors? Without such analysis, it is difficult to assess whether the anticipation mechanism is genuinely effective or merely plausible.

The paper would also benefit from stronger ablations overall. The proposed method has several ingredients: periodic synchronization tokens, deduplication, interpolation heuristic, three-stage training, synthetic data scale, chunk-size choice, and latency-aware user-chunk estimation. Yet the experiments mostly compare the full system against dGSLM and vary chunk size. Missing are ablations such as: no deduplication; deduplication without periodic sync tokens; direct modeling of raw HuBERT sequences; stage 3 only versus stages 1+2+3; synthetic data scale sensitivity; different TTS engines; and training without mixed text/speech sentence interleaving in stage 1. These are important because the paper’s contributions are modular, and the reader needs to know which components matter most.

A further concern is the fairness and informativeness of the baseline comparison. dGSLM is a reasonable historical baseline for full-duplex spoken dialogue, but it is also a speech-only model from an earlier paradigm and appears disadvantaged on semantic meaningfulness by design. The paper’s main empirical story is that a text-pretrained LLM has much better semantics than dGSLM; this is believable, but not surprising. The more interesting question is whether the proposed synchrony mechanism is competitive against stronger modern spoken-dialogue baselines, including cascaded streaming ASR + text LLM + TTS systems, or recent speech-text LLMs adapted for incremental interaction. The paper argues that prior systems are turn-based, which is fair, but a practical reviewer will still want to know whether the proposed approach improves over strong incremental or barge-in-capable cascaded systems in user-perceived interaction quality. Without such baselines, the empirical positioning feels somewhat narrow.

The semantic evaluation via ASR-transcribed generations and perplexity under a text dialogue model is also only partially convincing. First, the transcription explicitly ignores overlapping speech, which is central to the task. Second, perplexity under another model is a proxy for coherence, but it is not a standard or fully interpretable measure of dialogue quality. Third, the paper reports “perplexity drop relative to ground truth,” but the exact setup, reference model, and sensitivity to ASR errors deserve more detail. Since the human meaningfulness study is much more compelling, I would encourage the authors to rely less on this automatic metric or supplement it with stronger text-based semantic evaluations, such as response relevance judged by humans, transcript-level coherence ratings, or task-specific dialogue consistency measures.

The naturalness evaluation based on correlation of turn-taking event durations is interesting but somewhat limited. Correlating average durations of IPUs, pauses, and FTO with ground-truth continuations given the same prompt is a coarse statistic. It does not directly measure whether the model places backchannels appropriately, whether interruptions are pragmatically sensible, or whether overlap timing is locally well calibrated. A model could match global duration statistics while still producing awkward conversational dynamics. The human naturalness MOS partly addresses this, but the reported differences are small and sometimes favor the baseline slightly. More targeted analyses of overlap frequency, backchannel placement, interruption recovery, and response onset timing would strengthen the claim of human-like full-duplex behavior.

There are also some methodological ambiguities. The interpolation heuristic for reconstructing periodic HuBERT sequences from deduplicated chunks seems potentially lossy, especially for larger chunk sizes. The paper states that the effect is imperceptible, but this is asserted rather than demonstrated. Since speech quality is acknowledged as a limitation, it would help to quantify how much degradation comes from token interpolation versus the vocoder. Similarly, the choice of HuBERT at 25 Hz with a single codebook may constrain prosody and timing fidelity; this may be acceptable, but then claims about natural overlaps and backchannels should be tempered accordingly.

The use of synthetic speech data raises additional questions. Bark TTS with 10 speaker presets is used to generate a very large amount of synthetic dialogue. This is practical, but synthetic speech may have artifacts, limited prosodic diversity, and unnatural turn-taking cues. Since stage 2 explicitly constructs “full-duplex” data by pairing one speaker’s speech with silence on the other channel, it does not actually teach overlap behavior, only the formatting and within-utterance timing. The real overlap/backchannel behavior therefore comes almost entirely from the 2k hours of Fisher fine-tuning. This is not necessarily a problem, but it means the paper’s data-efficiency claim should be stated carefully: the synthetic data likely helps semantic grounding and sequence-format adaptation more than genuine duplex interaction skills. An ablation on stage 2 would clarify this.

Another limitation is the mismatch between the datasets and the claims about natural conversation. Fisher is telephone speech with its own conversational style and channel characteristics; CANDOR is more naturalistic but used mainly for testing and one interaction model. It is not obvious that the learned synchrony generalizes to broader conversational settings, multilingual dialogue, expressive speech, or noisy real-world audio. The paper does mention some of these limitations, but the main text occasionally overstates generality.

On presentation, the paper is generally readable and the core ideas are understandable, but there are places where the exposition could be tightened. Some claims are repeated across the introduction. A few implementation details that matter for reproducibility are missing or too brief: training durations, optimization hyperparameters, context lengths used in each stage, exact prompting/generation settings, how ASR is performed, how speaker activity thresholds are chosen, and how the interaction simulation is scheduled in wall-clock terms. Figure 7 is referenced but the image appears missing in the provided text, which is problematic because it supports an important claim about interaction-mode perplexity. There are also minor grammatical issues throughout.

I think the paper would be significantly stronger with the following additions or revisions. First, include a thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of synchronization tokens, deduplication, anticipation of the user chunk, and each training stage. Second, provide a more realistic interaction evaluation: either a small live user study with streaming inference, or at least an end-to-end latency analysis showing that chunk generation plus speech synthesis can actually meet the claimed timing constraints. Third, compare against a stronger practical baseline, ideally a streaming cascaded system with interruption handling or a recent speech-text LLM adapted for incremental response generation. Fourth, add more targeted full-duplex metrics, such as overlap rate, backchannel precision/recall relative to annotated events, response onset latency, and recovery after interruption. Fifth, clarify the semantic evaluation setup and reduce reliance on perplexity as the primary automatic measure.

In terms of significance, I do think the paper points toward an important direction. The idea that LLMs need an explicit temporal scaffold to participate in synchronous spoken interaction is insightful, and the proposed sequence formulation is simple enough that others may build on it. Even if some of the current evidence is preliminary, the work could stimulate more serious treatment of full-duplex interaction in speech-language modeling. The main question for acceptance is whether the current empirical support is strong enough for the breadth of the claims.

My overall assessment is positive but somewhat cautious. The paper has a novel and compelling core idea, a practical training recipe, and promising results, especially on semantic quality. However, the evaluation does not yet fully validate the strongest claims about real-time full-duplex interaction, and the lack of ablations makes it hard to attribute gains to the proposed mechanisms. If accepted, I would view it as an important early step toward synchronous spoken LLMs rather than a definitive solution to full-duplex dialogue.

I would lean toward a weak accept at a venue that values forward-looking systems ideas and emerging multimodal interaction paradigms, provided the authors can address some of the clarity and validation concerns. If the bar is very high on empirical completeness, I could also understand a borderline decision. The paper is interesting and potentially impactful, but it needs stronger experimental isolation and more realistic interaction evidence to fully substantiate its claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting a pretrained autoregressive text LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and latency-tolerant interaction. The core idea is to interleave two speakers’ speech-unit streams with periodic synchronization tokens that encode coarse timing, while deduplicating repeated HuBERT tokens to improve semantic efficiency. The model is trained in three stages: synthetic turn-based spoken dialogue from text data, synthetic full-duplex dialogue without overlaps, and finally real dual-channel spoken dialogue from Fisher. Experiments compare against dGSLM using semantic proxies (ASR-transcribed dialogue perplexity), turn-taking correlation metrics, and human MOS judgments. Results suggest substantially improved dialogue meaningfulness over dGSLM while maintaining similar naturalness, and some robustness to out-of-distribution data and simulated latency in LLM-LLM interaction.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving beyond turn-based spoken interfaces toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex dialogue.
The synchronization-token formulation is conceptually simple and compatible with standard autoregressive LLM architectures, enabling reuse of strong text-pretrained models.
The three-stage training recipe is practically motivated and leverages large-scale synthetic data to compensate for scarce real spoken dialogue data.
Empirical results show large gains in human-rated meaningfulness over the main baseline dGSLM, while preserving comparable naturalness.
Includes both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation (Fisher and CANDOR), which strengthens the generalization claims.
Considers latency explicitly and proposes a concrete mechanism for one-chunk-ahead user prediction to tolerate delayed inputs.
Human evaluation is reasonably broad for this area and reports uncertainty estimates.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is narrow: the main baseline is essentially only dGSLM, while comparisons to stronger modern speech-text or speech-dialogue LLM baselines are missing.
Several evaluation choices are indirect or potentially biased, especially semantic evaluation via ASR transcription followed by perplexity under a text dialogue model.
The claimed full-duplex interaction is only simulated via LLM-LLM interaction rather than demonstrated with real human users in live interactive settings.
The interpolation heuristic for reconstructing periodic HuBERT tokens from deduplicated chunks is ad hoc and not rigorously validated.
The paper does not provide enough ablations to isolate the contribution of key components such as synchronization tokens, deduplication, synthetic-data stages, chunk size, and user-chunk prediction.
Naturalness gains over dGSLM are modest, and in human evaluation SyncLLM is slightly below re-synthesized references and roughly at parity with dGSLM on naturalness.
The paper makes strong claims about Internet-scale latency robustness, but evaluation only covers simulated one-chunk latency and does not test realistic networking, ASR, or deployment effects.
methodological_flaws: The semantic metric is problematic: converting generated speech to text with ASR, discarding overlaps, and then scoring perplexity under a text-only dialogue model may systematically favor models whose outputs are easier for ASR/text models rather than genuinely better spoken dialogue models. This weakens the validity of the central meaningfulness claim.

The turn-taking evaluation computes Pearson correlation between average event durations in generations and ground-truth continuations conditioned on the same prompt. Correlation of averages is a weak proxy for conversational naturalness and does not establish that the generated timing distributions or event sequencing are realistic.

The latency-tolerance claim relies on simulated interaction between two models, not real-time interaction with humans or actual delayed streaming inputs. Thus the evidence does not fully support the practical claim of robust full-duplex deployment under Internet-scale latency.

The interpolation procedure assumes equal repetition of deduplicated tokens within a chunk when reconstructing periodic token streams. The paper acknowledges this is inaccurate but provides no objective analysis of reconstruction error or its downstream effect on synthesis quality and timing fidelity.

The comparison may not be fully controlled because dGSLM is a speech-only architecture while SyncLLM benefits from massive text-pretraining and large synthetic TTS-generated corpora. While this is a valid design choice, the paper sometimes frames the result as architectural superiority rather than a broader data/pretraining advantage.

The paper lacks statistical significance testing for many reported comparisons beyond confidence intervals in MOS tables, making it difficult to assess whether some improvements, especially in naturalness and chunk-size comparisons, are meaningful.

There is no rigorous validation that the model’s predicted user chunk improves interaction quality relative to simpler alternatives (e.g., waiting, speculative decoding variants, or direct next-agent prediction without explicit user estimation).
